Definition: Affordability of mobile broadband data, measured as the cost of a basic mobile data plan (1-2GB) as a percentage of GNI per capita. The UN Broadband Commission target is below 2% of monthly GNI per capita. Affordability is the single largest barrier to internet adoption in Africa.
revision_notes: The 2018 A4AI figure (8.76% regional average, not country-specific) is superseded by better country-level evidence but the conclusion is unchanged. ITU's 2024 'Measuring Digital Development' report groups CAR with Burundi, Chad and South Sudan as LDCs where the median data-only mobile-broadband basket exceeds 20% of monthly GNI per capita. A 2025 aggregation of ITU ICT pricing data (Africa API) puts CAR's mobile data basket at 53.7% of GNI per capita, the highest of any African country. Both sources place CAR well above the 10% threshold, confirming code 1.
revised_comments: Mobile data in the Central African Republic remains extremely expensive relative to income. ITU analysis groups the country among the least affordable LDC markets, with the cheapest data-only mobile-broadband basket priced at over 20% of monthly GNI per capita; a 2025 aggregation of ITU pricing data puts the figure at around 53.7% of GNI per capita, the highest of any African country. This is far above the UN Broadband Commission's 2% affordability target.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
revision_notes: ITU's March 2023 'Measuring Digital Development: Facts and Figures - Focus on LDCs' groups CAR in the lowest-connectivity LDC tier (with Burundi, Chad, DRC, Eritrea, Madagascar and others). The Digital Development Site (mAccess diagnostic tool, ITU-sourced) lists an almost identical 1.69 kbit/s per user figure to the original 1.6 kbit/s. No fresher official ITU figure was found reflecting CAR's fibre backbone connection to Cameroon and Congo (Central African Backbone project, completed September 2023), so the score is confirmed on the latest published international bandwidth data, which pre-dates the backbone coming into service.
revised_comments: International internet bandwidth per user in the Central African Republic remains among the lowest in the world at roughly 1.6-1.7 kbit/s per user, reflecting the country's historical reliance on costly satellite links and its position as one of the least-connected LDCs globally. Completion of the Central African Backbone fibre-optic link to Cameroon and the Republic of Congo in September 2023 is expected to improve bandwidth capacity, though this has not yet been reflected in published international bandwidth statistics.

Definition: Percentage of national population with access to electricity (grid or off-grid). This is the primary indicator of energy infrastructure availability for ICT. Based on World Bank/IEA Tracking SDG7 data, national statistical offices, or Afrobarometer surveys.
revision_notes: World Bank data (via TheGlobalEconomy.com, corroborated by ESMAP Tracking SDG7 and CountryDataHub, both citing World Bank Open Data series EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS) confirm national electricity access at 17.6% in 2023, up from 15.7% in 2022. Urban access was 37.4% and rural access just 2.3% in 2023. This remains well within the <25% band, confirming code 1.
revised_comments: National electricity access in the Central African Republic stood at 17.6% of the population in 2023 according to World Bank data, among the lowest rates in the world. Access is heavily concentrated in urban areas (37.4% in 2023) while rural access remains minimal at 2.3%.

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
Value Name: Severe (frequent daily outages or regular load shedding)
revision_notes: World Bank Enterprise Survey data (via CEIC) show CAR firms experienced an average of 28.3 power outages per month in 2023 (near-daily), with 89.3% of firms reporting electrical outages, confirming severe, frequent disruption consistent with code 1. The original World Bank project appraisal document (2022) cited blackouts of 16-18 hours per day pre-project. A March 2025 news report on prolonged multi-day blackouts in Bangui indicates the national picture remains severe despite the 2023 Danzi solar plant commissioning, though the World Bank reports localised improvements in Bangui specifically since then. On balance the evidence still supports 'Severe' rather than an improved category.
revised_comments: Power supply in the Central African Republic remains highly unreliable. World Bank Enterprise Survey data for 2023 show firms experiencing an average of around 28 power outages per month, with the large majority of firms affected by outages. Bangui has continued to experience prolonged multi-day blackouts as recently as 2025, reflecting persistent structural weaknesses in generation and transmission, notwithstanding recent solar investments such as the Danzi plant.
